children.text: Mount Isarog is a stratovolcano rising behind Naga City in Camarines Sur, famous for a two-day trek through mossy forest and past waterfalls to a summit of about 1,966–2,000 m. It is protected as Mount Isarog Natural Park, and climbing requires a permit from the Naga City government and a guide.

Mount Isarog is a stratovolcano in Camarines Sur in the Bicol region of southeastern Luzon. It rises on the isthmus between Lagonoy Gulf and San Miguel Bay, and Wikipedia gives its height as about 2,000 m while the hiking site Pinoy Mountaineer lists 1,966 m (plus). Near the summit, the boundaries of several local governments meet: Goa, Tigaon, Ocampo, Pili, Naga City, Tinambac and Calabanga. It belongs to the Bicol volcanic arc, and from the summit you can see the crater, the coast of the Bicol peninsula and Mayon Volcano to the south.

The mountain was proclaimed a national park in 1938 and was redesignated in 2002 as a protected area, Mount Isarog Natural Park. Vegetation changes clearly with altitude, from lowland tropical forest through grassland and montane forest to mossy forest above about 1,500 m. The mossy forest has a low canopy of 2–6 m, covered with moss, pitcher plants, orchids and ferns. Wikipedia says the mountain is home to endemic species such as the Isarog shrew rat (Rhynchomys isarogensis) and has 15 bird species endemic to Luzon. Wikipedia also divides the vegetation into lowland forest at about 500–900 m, grassland (cogon and talahib grass) at 700–1,200 m, montane forest at 1,000–1,400 m and mossy forest above 1,500 m. One hiking guide says there are more than 1,300 plant species and that rafflesia has been sighted.

You need a permit from the Investment and Tourism Promotions Office (ITPO) of Naga City Hall to climb. According to the city's guidelines, summit climbs on the Panicuason trail are always two days, limited to 20 hikers a day, with one guide required for every five hikers. You cannot reach the summit as a day hike; you camp overnight at Camp 4 and head for the summit at dawn. A 2026 guide rates the difficulty at 5–6 out of 9 and does not recommend it for beginners.

The mountain's appeal is its accessibility. From the trailhead, which you can reach from Naga by jeepney and tricycle, you get forest, waterfalls, camping and a sunrise ridge in one trip. In the rainy season, however, the path is slippery and leeches are common, which makes it harder. Permit procedures and fees change often, so check the Naga City government's latest announcements before you go.

This is the most widely used official trail, and it starts near the DENR station in Panicuason, Naga City. One guide gives the starting elevation as about 350 m and describes walking from the entrance to the summit over two days.

Malabsay Falls and Nabuntalan Falls come early on the trail, and Malabsay is described as the first highlight, with a large catch basin. One guide says you can see the waterfalls on the way to Camp 1.

Above about 1,500 m the trees get lower and the forest is covered with moss and liverworts. The atmosphere on a misty day is especially striking, and orchids and pitcher plants can also be seen. It gets cooler as you climb, so a light jacket is useful at dawn.
The summit climb starts from Camp 4 at dawn. A 2026 guide describes leaving at 05:00 and reaching the crater rim at about 06:30. On a clear day you can see Lagonoy Gulf, Naga and the Mayon area.
Sources mention endemic rodents such as the Isarog shrew rat, bird species endemic to Luzon, and amphibians such as the Isarog cloud frog. If you meet wildlife, do not feed or touch it.
One review says you can soothe tired muscles in the Panicuason hot springs after the descent. As befits a volcanic area, there are said to be hot springs and signs of gas seepage.
There are six numbered campsites, and summit climbers sleep at Camp 4. Streams run from Camp 1 to Camp 6, but flow can drop in the dry months of March to May, so ask your guide.
Before or after the climb you can plan a day in Naga City for Peñafrancia devotion sites and city food. If the climb is too demanding, you can also go only as far as the waterfalls.

children.text: Confirm your permit and guide assignment at the ITPO (Room 207, 2nd floor) at Naga City Hall. One review says permit and payment must be completed before you arrive and walk-ins on the morning of the climb are not accepted.
Take a jeepney or tricycle to the DENR station in Panicuason and meet your guide.
Start the trek. If you wish, visit Malabsay Falls first.
Refill your water and rest at Camp 1 (about 935 m).
Pass Camp 2 (about 1,200 m).
Arrive at Camp 4, pitch your tent and have dinner. One guide says it takes about
6 hours
from the entrance to Camp 4.
On the second day, leave Camp 4 at dawn for the summit.
Enjoy views of Lagonoy Gulf, Naga and the Mayon direction from the crater rim.
Return to Camp 4, have breakfast, pack up and descend. One guide says the descent takes about
3–4 hours
When you reach the station, rest at the Panicuason hot springs.
This schedule is an example based on one 2026 review, and it varies greatly with your group's pace and the weather. Follow your guide's instructions.

children.text: Travel from Naga city proper to Panicuason.
Confirm your official permit and guide at the DENR station. Ask the ITPO about the rules for routes that are not summit climbs.
Walk to the area around Malabsay Falls and take photos.
Rest at the hot springs and return to Naga City.
The entry rules for sections other than the summit climb could not be confirmed, so be sure to ask the ITPO first.
Overnight buses run from Manila (PITX and Cubao) to Naga, and the ride takes about
8–10 hours
(DLTB lists 8–9 hours; Isarog Line about 10). Because the ITPO opens at 8:00 a.m., a departure between 19:00 and 21:00 is typical.
Per 2026 operator listings, one-way fares are about
for regular air-conditioned buses and
for Lazyboy to Skybus premium seats (Isarog Line regular ₱950, DLTB regular from ₱912; fuel surcharges may raise them). Check before you go.
From central Naga (near the market), take a jeepney or tricycle to Panicuason, then a motorcycle taxi or a chartered tricycle to the DENR station gate.
The ITPO at Naga City Hall (Room 207) is where you obtain your climbing permit. The phone is (054) 205-2980 ext. 1130, and the email is tourism@naga.gov.ph.
Naga Airport (WNP) is the nearest, but routes and service change often. Check the latest schedules.
From Bicol International Airport (DRP) you have to continue to Naga overland, so allow extra time.
The Patag-Patag trail is described as a steeper route up from the east. Other trails may have different entry rules, so confirm the permit procedure first.

The December–April dry season is best. A 2026 guide says this period has relatively little rain and a lower typhoon risk, though the trail is still muddy. From March to May, campsite water can run low, so ask your guide about the water situation.

Naga gets very crowded during the Peñafrancia Festival in September, so book lodging and transport early if you climb then. One guide also says the city can suspend permits when a typhoon signal is raised over Camarines Sur.

There is almost no lodging in Panicuason at the foot of the mountain, so most climbers stay in Naga City and travel at dawn. You need to be at City Hall by 8:00 a.m., when the ITPO opens, to confirm your permit, so a city-center hotel is convenient. Room rates vary by date, so check a booking site.

There is nowhere to resupply on the mountain, so you must carry two days of food yourself. Before you leave, buy ready-to-eat food, energy bars and nuts at a Naga market or store. After the climb, try Bicolano food in Naga City. Dishes simmered in coconut milk and spicy sauces are the region's signature.

If the climb feels too demanding, resting a day in Naga City and simply looking up at the mountain is meaningful enough. This mountain, rising close to Naga City, is both a symbol of the area's scenery and a natural park. When planning, it is safest to check first whether permit slots are available and then book transport and lodging.
Complete your permit and payment before you leave. You need an online application, a signed waiver and scans of your IDs.
You need one guide per five hikers, and two guides for six. Gathering companions to share costs lowers the cost per person.
Bring rain gear, leech socks and knee-high gaiters. Leeches are plentiful in the rainy season.
For the dawn summit push, you need a warm mid-layer and a headlamp.
Mobile signal is weak in the forest, so download offline maps in Naga.
Use a sturdy tent. One review says the ground at the campsite can flood when it rains.
Bring two days of food and enough water bottles. One guide says there are no proper toilets or showers at the camps.
The limit is 20 hikers a day, so keep your schedule flexible.
A permit and guide are required for a summit climb, and permits may be suspended when a typhoon signal is raised. The climb is hard, so go with enough fitness and the right gear.
The difficulty is 5–6 out of 9 and the trail is slippery. Beginners should gain experience on other mountains first.
There are many leeches and insects in the forest, and the path turns to mud when it rains.
It is a volcanic area with gas seepage and hot springs. Do not enter places that your guide does not allow.
Do not plan a descent that ends late in the afternoon. It gets dark early in the forest.
Permit procedures and fees may change, so check the Naga City government's latest announcements.
The gateway city to Mount Isarog, with lodging, restaurants and the permit office.
A cathedral in the center of Naga City, worth a visit before or after the climb.
A major festival held in Naga City every September. Lodging and transport get crowded then.
The perfectly cone-shaped volcano visible to the south from the Isarog summit.
The main city of Albay, a good continuation to the south after the Isarog climb.
